items.title: Sea Urchins Wearing Hats
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
The sight of a spiky sea urchins wandering along the floor of the ocean wearing a hat is pretty funny, and even more so when it's a bunch of them (I don't know the collective noun for sea urchins) all wearing a variety of hats that are really rocks, shells, and other ocean debris. One even carries a shell with a hermit crab living in it! But why do they do that? And how did they learn this new behavior? 

In this clip from the new BBC nature series Blue Planet III, Sir David Attenborough narrates a sea urchin fashion show and explains what benefit this adaptation gives these brainless sea creatures. (via Born in Space)

items.title: Why I Don't Like Rom-Coms
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content: One reason I never really liked rom-coms is that there is rarely any comedy in them. And even more so, the fact that the lead character's "happy ending" is so often ending up with the guy who ruined her life, or at least treated her terribly. Oh, I liked those stories when I was young and desired the bad boy. A few bad boys later, I understand that these romantic victories are altogether a horrible idea for lasting happiness. I agree with this host's insight, at least in the movies here that I've seen, which is a minority of them.

items.title: The Nazca Booby
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
The Galápagos Islands are a unique places for animals. Most of the area is a national park, fiercely protected, and the creatures who live there never had to worry about a threat from humans. So those who are lucky enough to visit can get up close and personal with seals, reptiles, tortoises, and birds such a boobies. 

Nazca booby is one such bird that nests in the Galápagos. They are great swimmers, but a bit awkward on land with their big feet. In this video, we see how they court and set up nests, although they can get confused as to which nest is theirs, and which mate is theirs. This can cause a bit of problem. But even stranger is their "heir and a spare" system of raising chicks. With limited resources, they can only successfully raise one chick. Yet they lay two eggs at a time. The chicks themselves will have to decide who is the favorite.

items.title: The Myths About Disneyland's Feral Cats
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
You've heard that Disneyland has a huge colony of cats who roam the park at night, hunting mice and other rodents who come in to get a meal from the trash people leave behind. The company doesn't talk about it because, after all, their mascot is a mouse. And specifically because Disney doesn't talk about those cats (much), internet legends have grown up around them.

The cats moved in on their own because they found shelter where they wouldn't be bothered by people. Yes, they are managed by the park's administration now, but that was a gradual shift over time, and doesn't happen in the way you've been told. Cats don't follow instructions, especially feral cats. The Imagination Files dug into the history of these cats and busts some myths. The one thing he doesn't tell us is who gets to clean the litter boxes.

items.title: The Man Under the City
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
The strongest man in the world has given all for his queen. There is definitely some kind of relationship there, so they trade wishes. The queen wishes for the man to bear the burden of her city on his back. And so he does. He takes the brunt of attacks from rival armies and mythical monsters, through all kinds of weather, while she and her court enjoy the high ground. There is strategy in the upper reaches, and we even see a contrasting style to illustrate how disconnected the top is with the bottom. We know what the queen's wish is, but what is our hero's wish? We aren't going to find out, because this story does not end the way you expect it to.

The animated story of The Man Under the City has layers of morality that go deeper the more you think about them. But creator DoodletmeGO tells us this is only one chapter in the legend of the strongest man in the world. (via

items.title: Dangerous Self-Experiments That Paid Off
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Our idea of a mad scientist is one who has nefarious aims while conducting experiments, which is convenient for serving as a villain in a story. It's more common in real life that a scientist is trying to advance knowledge and make the world a better place, but some of them can be a little crazy, or at least somewhat reckless. Today we have ethics boards that stop dangerous experiments and make sure we keep subjects informed of risks. What's an ethical scientist to do? In some cases, when an experiment is just too risky to ask someone else to be a subject, the scientist will try it on themself. That takes both confidence and guts.  

We've seen scientists and engineers try out something new that failed spectacularly, leading to their deaths (early flying machines come to mind). But there are a few cases in which these self-experiments led to great scientific breakthroughs, and sometimes even a Nobel Prize. This TED-Ed lesson brings us several such stories. Oh, and don't try this at home.

items.title: Autumn vs. Fall
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Now that we are two-thirds of the way through the season, we need to discuss what we call it. Do you say "autumn" or "fall"? As Laurence Brown points out, Americans understand the terms interchangeably even though we use fall most often, while the British insist that it's autumn and that's the only correct term. Why is this important? I don't know. Anyway, Brown gives us the origins of each term, which makes more sense in American English because we have a lot of deciduous trees, and when the leaves fall, they are spectacular. Autumn, on the other hand, is a made up word. That doesn't make it bad, just different.   

In true American form, Brown believes that both terms are correct. This leads him to a rant about how stupid it is to argue about the different way countries use the same language. This video has a skippable ad from 1:28 to 2:48.

items.title: The Mathematical Way to Slice a Rectangular Cake
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Kids at a birthday party love cake, but they will argue with you about which slice they want, since the corners have the most frosting. How can you slice a rectangular sheet cake to make it fair to everyone? That involves math, or at least geometry. This solution came from ZhenChao Wu in 1998. This guy says it will work for any number of guests, but when you think about it, that only goes for even numbers. You can always round up to the next even number, and put the last piece away for later.  

However, most birthday parties also have adults attending. What this solution doesn't take into account is that some people do not prefer a lot of icing on their slice, especially in a store-bought sheet cake. And if being fair to the kids is the goal, you can always have a round cake. Personally, I always made more cake than needed, because homemade cakes are always good the next day. (via Laughing Squid)

items.title: The Sun's Calories
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
The latest "dumb" theoretical question for the What If? series by Randall Munroe and Henry Reich has to do with the amount of calories the sun sends us in ratio to the calories in the food we consume. On the surface, that sounds like comparing apples to oranges, but a calorie is a unit of energy. They did the math and there are some extremely large numbers here, but suffice it to say that the sun provides enough energy to feed billions of people on a lot of earth-like planets. Plants are rather good at harvesting this energy, at least enough to keep us fed, but an awful lot of the sun's energy that reaches earth is wasted. And that's even after taking into account that some of us consume way too many calories. Not that the sun cares; it will just keep burning for a few more billion years.

items.title: Thanksgiving Logistics
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Here's a friendly reminder that if you have a frozen turkey over 12 pounds, you should put it in the refrigerator to begin thawing today. If it's 12 pounds or smaller, you might be able to wait until Sunday or Monday. I got my 18-pounder out yesterday, because I've done this quite a few times.

If you are new to cooking Thanksgiving, this might be a good time to jot down your to-do list for the next week. Anything that can be prepared ahead of time, while keeping in mind how fresh it must be, should be listed on the appropriate day. For example, make cornbread on Tuesday, make the cornbread into dressing on Wednesday night, pop it in the oven Thursday. Remember, you will not have a lot of oven room with a turkey in there Thursday, so make sure your pies are done before cooking the bird. You may as well shop for everything you need now, except for fresh produce.

The one thing I forget every year is to take the second oven rack out of the oven before heating. I always have to remove a hot rack and set it out on the deck so no one gets burned. But that doesn't ruin any food, so I feel good that it's my one constant failure.

Oh, there will be other failures. Any big production, like a wedding, will have something go wrong. It's best just to laugh it off, because without a glitch or two, it would be hard to recall these occasions in future years.

items.title: A Unique Piece of Amber
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Amber is hardened and fossilized tree resin. When resin (which is different from sap) falls on an animal, usually an insect, that body is preserved as is. That allows us to see prehistoric bugs as they appeared in life, with its original form preserved even if it is dessicated, encased in nature's glass.

This cricket encased in amber is a rare specimen, because it has a tiny gas bubble still in its abdomen. The bubble was most likely formed by chemical and bacterial action on whatever the cricket last ate, and it might be methane. In other words, it's a fart. It couldn't be expelled because resin is pretty thick before it turns to stone, and the cricket was dead anyway. But this bubble still moves when you turn the amber! That requires liquid, and with a little digging I found out that amber can contain water despite the resin's dehydrating properties under certain conditions. Cool. (via Geeks Are Sexy)

items.title: Trying to Avoid a Cold
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Cold and flu season are ramping up, so let's take two minutes to consider something you've never really thought about before. Where is the place you are most likely to run into someone who has a communicable illness? In bed, sure, but you can avoid other people's beds. You might say the doctor's office, but if you're willing to spend your time and money there, that means you're already pretty sick (at least in America). No, it's the store aisle where the cold remedies are. When there's a bug going around, that aisle is liable to be crowded with suspicious shoppers. You could order symptom relief through Door Dash, but those gig workers are desperate enough to work while sick, and will sneeze on your package.

items.title: Rich People Collecting Unicorn Horns
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Once you have enough money to buy all the fine objects and comforts available to you, the rich are left with a desire to be admired by others. The easy way to do that is to buy more stuff, as long as those objects are rare, expensive, and liable to draw attention. In the 16th and 17th centuries, there was a world of these curious objects available from world explorers and traders. Wealthy people collected exotic art from faraway places and natural specimens never seen before, or even better both in one object, into curiosity cabinets. Explaining these impressive objects raised one's status in a way mere money didn't, even when that explanation was nonsense. Evan Puschak explores the rise of curiosity cabinets and the forces that made them a thing. (via kottke)

items.title: Authoritarian Fiction is Scarier Than Post-Apocalypse Dystopias
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Grim stories about the future come in two basic models. Some are about apocalyptic disasters, like a zombie uprising, an alien invasion, or a nuclear war that wipes out most of mankind, leaving our protagonists to figure out how to survive and start all over. That would include things like Mad Max, A Boy and His Dog, The Book of Eli, and I Am Legend. 

Then there's the authoritarian dystopia, in which the population is still here, but kept under the thumb of an authoritarian government. The classic example is 1984, but it would also include Soylent Green, The Handmaid's Tale, The Hunger Games, and Wall-E. These stories are actually scarier, because they could more plausibly come true. In fact, most are based at least partly on events that have already happened somewhere at some time. To sum it up, apocalyptic disasters rely heavily on fantasy, while authoritarian fiction is a warning of what could happen if we aren't diligent. PBS picks these stories apart, and shows us how we might still slide down those paths.
